newsitem.title: USA: Fund holders seem unfazed by U.S. market downturn.
newsitem.headline: Fund holders seem unfazed by U.S. market downturn.

text.p: Mutual fund companies reported busy phone lines on Monday, but investors seemed more concerned about taxes and retirement plans than the recent market volatility, officials said.
Phone volume was up about 10 percent at Charles Schwab & Co, whose representatives answer about 90,000 calls daily and another 250,000 by automation, spokeswoman Tracey Gordon said.
"Has the world ended? No," Gordon said. "There are people buying, there are people selling, there are people calling to check quotes. It's all over the place."
Charles Schwab & Co, a unit of Charles Schwab Corp, sells more than 2,000 mutual funds from a wide number of companies through its mutual fund supermarket.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 157 points or more than 2.3 percent to 6,583 on Monday on the heels of Thursday's 140-point drop.
A spokesman for Vanguard Group said many investors were calling with questions about Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) before the April 15 tax deadline.
"It's just another typical Monday for us," Vanguard spokesman Brian Mattes said.
"So far, you can't tell by our phone volumes or the nature of our phone calls that there's anything unusual happening in the stock market at all," Mattes said.
Boston-based Putnam Investments had average phone volumes on Monday, and most investors had quick questions, spokesman Matthew Keenan said.
"Ninety percent of the calls we have been getting have been answered in 20 seconds. It doesn't apppear to be any increase from normal," he said.

A spokesman for Fidelity Investments, the largest mutual fund company in the country, said calls were slightly higher last Thursday, mostly due to questions about IRAs. He had no information about calls on Monday.
"This is typically a busy time of year. Customers are calling with tax-related questions and they're opening retirement accounts," spokesman Scott Beyerl said.
